levels.title: Money foundations
levels.summary: Where your money goes, why a cash cushion comes first, and how debt and credit work. Free for everyone.

modules.title: Where your money goes
modules.summary: What comes in, what goes out, and a plan you can keep.

lessons.title: What a budget is actually for
objectives: Explain a budget as a plan for your money, not a punishment
List the three buckets most budgets use
key_points: A budget is a plan you make before the month starts
Most budgets split money into needs, wants and future you
A plan you can keep beats a perfect plan you quit

try_it.prompt: Write down your monthly take-home pay and your three biggest costs.

quiz.q: What is a budget mainly for?
choices: Planning where your money goes before you spend it
quiz.why: A budget is a plan made ahead of time.

quiz.q: Which bucket is ‘future you’?
quiz.why: Future you covers saving and paying down debt.

quiz.q: Which budget usually works best?
quiz.why: Consistency matters more than perfection.

lessons.title: Reading your paycheck: gross pay, take-home pay and deductions
objectives: Tell the difference between gross pay and take-home pay
Name the common deductions on a pay stub
key_points: Gross pay is what you earn; take-home pay is what lands in your account
Income tax, Social Security and Medicare are taken out before you see the money
Benefits like health insurance and retirement savings can come out too

try_it.prompt: Find your last pay stub and enter your gross pay, take-home pay and three biggest deductions.

quiz.q: What is take-home pay?
choices: What's left after taxes and other deductions
quiz.why: Take-home (net) pay is what actually reaches your account.

quiz.q: Which of these usually comes out of a paycheck before you get it?
quiz.why: Employers withhold income tax, Social Security and Medicare from each paycheck.

quiz.q: Why plan with take-home pay instead of gross pay?
choices: It's the money you can actually spend or save
quiz.why: You can only budget money that actually reaches you.

lessons.title: Tracking a month of spending, without the guilt
objectives: Explain why tracking comes before cutting
Sort spending into fixed costs and flexible costs
key_points: Track one normal month before you change anything
Fixed costs stay the same; flexible costs are where change is easiest
Small repeat costs, like subscriptions, add up over a year

try_it.prompt: Go through last month's bank and card statements and total your fixed and flexible costs.

quiz.q: What's the point of tracking a month of spending?
choices: To feel bad about past choices
To see where money actually goes before you plan
quiz.why: Real numbers make a better plan than guesses.

quiz.q: Which is usually a flexible cost?
quiz.why: Flexible costs change month to month, so they're the easiest to adjust.

quiz.q: A $15 monthly subscription costs about how much a year?
quiz.why: $15 a month times 12 months is $180.

modules.title: Your safety net
modules.summary: Why a cash cushion comes first, and where to keep it.

lessons.title: Why a cash cushion comes first
objectives: Explain what an emergency cushion is for
Explain why money you need soon shouldn't be in the stock market
key_points: A cushion covers surprises so they don't become debt
Money you may need soon has no time to recover from a drop
Start small: even one month of costs helps
lessons.risk_note: Stock prices can drop at any time, which is why money needed soon is often kept in savings instead.

try_it.prompt: Add up one month of must-pay costs. That's your first cushion target.

quiz.q: What is an emergency cushion for?
quiz.why: It keeps surprises from turning into debt.

quiz.q: Why keep it out of the stock market?
choices: Stocks can only be sold once a year
You may need it right when prices are down
quiz.why: Short-term money has no time to recover from a drop.

quiz.q: A good first target is…
quiz.why: Start with a goal you can reach.

lessons.title: Where to keep your cushion
objectives: Compare checking and savings accounts for a cash cushion
Explain what deposit insurance does
key_points: A separate savings account keeps the cushion easy to reach but less tempting to spend
Savings accounts pay interest, and rates differ a lot between banks
Government deposit insurance protects money at insured banks and credit unions, up to a limit

try_it.prompt: Note where your cushion lives now, its interest rate, and whether the bank or credit union is insured.

quiz.q: Why keep a cushion in a separate savings account?
choices: It pays exactly the same as checking
It's easy to reach but less tempting to spend
quiz.why: Separation makes the cushion harder to spend by accident.

quiz.q: What does deposit insurance do?
choices: Protects deposits at an insured bank or credit union, up to a limit, if it fails
Covers money lost to impulse spending
quiz.why: It protects your deposits if an insured institution fails, up to the legal limit.

quiz.q: Interest rates on savings accounts…
choices: Are set by law and identical everywhere
Can differ a lot from bank to bank
quiz.why: Rates vary, so it's worth comparing.

modules.title: Debt and credit
modules.summary: How interest on debt works, ways to pay it down, and what a credit score measures.

lessons.title: How credit card interest really works
objectives: Explain what an APR is
Explain why paying only the minimum keeps debt around for years
key_points: APR is the yearly interest rate charged on a balance you carry
Paying only the minimum can keep a balance around for years
Paying the full statement balance by the due date usually avoids interest on purchases

try_it.prompt: List each debt with its balance, interest rate and minimum payment.

quiz.q: What is a card's APR?
choices: The yearly interest rate on a balance you carry
The fee for opening the card
quiz.why: APR means annual percentage rate: the yearly cost of carrying a balance.

quiz.q: If you carry a balance, what happens to the interest charged?
choices: It disappears at the end of the year
It's added to what you owe
The bank pays it for you
quiz.why: Interest is added to the balance, so unpaid interest can grow too.

quiz.q: Paying only the minimum each month usually means…
choices: The debt is gone within a month
The debt can last for years and cost more in interest
quiz.why: Minimum payments mostly cover interest, so the balance shrinks slowly.

lessons.title: Paying down debt: avalanche or snowball
objectives: Describe the avalanche and snowball approaches
Explain the trade-off between saving interest and staying motivated
key_points: Avalanche: pay extra on the highest-rate debt first, which usually saves the most interest
Snowball: pay extra on the smallest balance first, for quick wins
Either way, keep paying at least the minimum on every debt

try_it.prompt: Sort your debts by interest rate and by balance, and see which one each approach would tackle first.

quiz.q: The avalanche approach pays extra on…
quiz.why: Avalanche targets the most expensive debt first.

quiz.q: What's the main appeal of the snowball approach?
choices: It always costs the least interest
Quick wins that help people stay motivated
quiz.why: Clearing small balances fast can keep people going.

quiz.q: While focusing on one debt, what happens with the others?
choices: Keep paying at least the minimum on each
quiz.why: Missing minimums brings fees and can hurt your credit.

lessons.title: What a credit score is, and what moves it
objectives: Explain what a credit score measures and why lenders use it
Name the habits that affect a score most
key_points: A credit score sums up how you've handled borrowing, based on your credit reports
Paying on time and keeping balances low compared with your limits matter most
Checking your own credit reports is free and doesn't lower your score

try_it.prompt: Note when you last checked your credit reports, and set a reminder to check them again.

quiz.q: A credit score is mainly based on…
quiz.why: Scores are calculated from the borrowing history in your credit reports.

quiz.q: Which habit tends to help a score most?
choices: Opening many new cards at once
Using all of your credit limit
quiz.why: On-time payment history is one of the biggest parts of a score.

quiz.q: Does checking your own credit report lower your score?
choices: Yes, if you check more than once a year
No, checking your own report doesn't affect it
quiz.why: Checking your own report is a ‘soft’ check that doesn't change your score.

lessons.title: Paying down a card or investing: comparing the math
objectives: Compare a debt's interest rate with uncertain investment growth
Explain why many people pay off high-interest debt before investing
key_points: Paying off a card saves its interest rate, with no market ups and downs
Investment growth isn't certain and can be negative in any year
Many people keep a small cushion, clear high-interest debt, then invest
lessons.risk_note: Investments can fall in value, including the money you put in. This is general education, not advice for your situation.

try_it.prompt: Next to each debt in your Money Map, write its interest rate, and circle any in double digits.

quiz.q: Paying off a card with a high interest rate is a bit like…
choices: Earning that rate, without market swings
quiz.why: Every dollar paid off stops that interest from being charged.

quiz.q: Why is investment growth hard to compare with a debt's rate?
choices: It's fixed in advance, like a loan rate
It's never certain and can be negative
quiz.why: A debt's rate is known; investment results aren't.

quiz.q: What order do many people follow?
choices: A small cushion, then high-interest debt, then investing
Invest first, then deal with debt
Skip the cushion and invest everything
quiz.why: A cushion prevents new debt, and clearing costly debt comes next for many people.

levels.title: Your first investments
levels.summary: What investing is, how growth and risk go together, and what you pay along the way.

modules.title: How growth and risk work
modules.summary: Owning vs. lending, why time matters, and why prices swing.

lessons.title: What investing is: owning and lending
objectives: Explain the difference between owning (stocks) and lending (bonds)
Explain why investing is for money you won't need for years
key_points: A stock is a small piece of ownership in a company
A bond is a loan to a company or government that pays interest
Investing is for money you can leave alone for years, because prices can drop
lessons.risk_note: Stocks and bonds can both lose value, including the money you put in.

try_it.prompt: Mark which of your goals are more than five years away.

quiz.q: Buying a share of stock means…
choices: Owning a small piece of a company
quiz.why: A share is a slice of ownership.

quiz.q: Buying a bond means…
choices: Lending money that's paid back with interest, if the borrower can pay
quiz.why: A bond is a loan, and the borrower might not be able to pay.

quiz.q: Why is investing usually for money you won't need soon?
choices: Prices can drop, and money needed soon might have to be sold low
Investment accounts are locked for 30 years
quiz.why: Time gives more room to wait out a drop.

lessons.title: Compound growth, explained with $100 a month
objectives: Explain compound growth in plain words
Explain why starting earlier matters
key_points: Growth can earn growth of its own over time
Starting earlier gives money more years to grow
Growth is never promised: investments can lose value
lessons.risk_note: Examples are hypothetical. Investments can fall in value, including the money you put in.

try_it.prompt: Compare starting at your age with starting 5 years later.

quiz.q: Compound growth means…
choices: Your gains can earn gains of their own
Your bank pays a fixed bonus
quiz.why: Growth builds on earlier growth.

quiz.q: Why does starting earlier matter?
choices: Early money gets more years to grow
Taxes are lower for young people
quiz.why: Time is the input you control most.

quiz.q: Which is true about investment growth?
choices: It only happens in savings accounts
quiz.why: Every investment carries risk.

lessons.title: What “risk” actually means when you invest
objectives: Explain volatility as how much prices swing
Explain the link between risk and potential return
Explain how time horizon changes how much a drop matters
key_points: Risk means prices can swing, and you can lose money, including what you put in
Investments with higher potential returns usually come with bigger swings
Money needed soon has less time to wait out a drop
lessons.risk_note: Past swings don't tell you future ones. Any investment can lose value.

try_it.prompt: Turn on “Show a market drop” and compare a drop near the start with one near the end.

quiz.q: Volatility describes…
choices: How much and how fast prices swing
quiz.why: Volatility is the size and speed of price swings.

quiz.q: Investments with higher potential returns usually…
choices: Come with bigger swings and more chance of loss
quiz.why: Higher potential reward usually means more risk.

quiz.q: Why does a drop matter more for money you need next year?
choices: Drops only happen to long-term money
There's little time to wait out the drop
quiz.why: Short-term money may have to be used while prices are down.

modules.title: Spreading risk
modules.summary: Why one company is risky, and how funds spread money across many.

lessons.title: Diversification: not keeping all your eggs in one basket
objectives: Explain diversification in plain words
Explain why one company's bad news hurts less when you own many
key_points: Diversification means spreading money across many investments
One company's bad news matters less when it's a small part of what you own
It lowers some risk, but a whole market can still fall together
lessons.risk_note: Diversification can reduce risk but doesn't remove it. Diversified investments can still lose value.

try_it.prompt: Note anywhere your money is concentrated in one place, such as one company or one account.

quiz.q: Diversification means…
choices: Putting all your money in one great company
quiz.why: It spreads risk across many holdings.

quiz.q: Why does diversification help?
choices: One company's trouble is a smaller part of the whole
quiz.why: No single company can sink the whole portfolio.

quiz.q: Can a diversified portfolio still lose value?
choices: Yes, a whole market can fall together
Only if you check it daily
quiz.why: Diversification doesn't protect against a market-wide drop.

lessons.title: What a fund is: mutual funds and ETFs
objectives: Explain how a fund pools money to buy many investments
Tell the difference between a mutual fund and an ETF
key_points: A fund pools money from many people to buy many investments at once
Mutual funds trade once a day at a set price; ETFs trade during the day like stocks
Every fund charges a yearly fee, shown as its expense ratio
lessons.risk_note: Funds can lose value. A fund's past results don't predict its future.

try_it.prompt: Next time you see a fund's name, look for its expense ratio and what it holds.

quiz.q: What does a fund do?
choices: Pools money to buy many investments
quiz.why: A fund combines many people's money into one basket of investments.

quiz.q: One difference between ETFs and mutual funds is…
choices: ETFs trade during the day; mutual funds trade once a day
ETFs are insured by the government
quiz.why: Mutual funds are priced once a day after markets close.

quiz.q: A fund's expense ratio is…
choices: Its yearly fee, as a share of the money invested
quiz.why: The expense ratio is the yearly cost of owning the fund.

lessons.title: Index funds vs. single stocks: what's the difference?
objectives: Explain what an index fund tracks
Compare the risk of one stock with the risk of a broad index fund
key_points: An index fund aims to match a market index instead of picking winners
A single stock depends on one company; a broad index fund spreads across many
Index funds still fall when the market falls
lessons.risk_note: Index funds and single stocks can both lose value. This lesson compares how they work; it doesn't recommend either.

try_it.prompt: Run a hypothetical crash with the pretend index portfolio and note its lowest point.

quiz.q: An index fund tries to…
quiz.why: Index funds aim to track an index, not beat it.

quiz.q: Which carries more single-company risk?
quiz.why: One stock depends entirely on one company.

quiz.q: When the overall market falls, a broad index fund…
quiz.why: A broad index fund holds the market, so it moves with it.

modules.title: Costs and accounts
modules.summary: What investing costs, and the kinds of accounts that hold investments.

lessons.title: How a 1% fee adds up over time
objectives: Name common investing fees
Explain why a small yearly fee matters over decades
key_points: Common fees include fund expense ratios, advisory fees and trading costs
A yearly fee is charged whether the investment gained or lost
Over decades, a small yearly fee can make a big difference, because money paid in fees can't grow
lessons.risk_note: The 1% fee is a hypothetical example. Growth isn't certain, and fees apply even when investments lose value.

try_it.prompt: Run your numbers, then lower the growth rate by 1 point to see roughly what a 1% yearly fee could cost.

quiz.q: When is a fund's yearly fee charged?
choices: Every year, in good years and bad
quiz.why: Fees don't depend on results.

quiz.q: Why can a 1% fee matter so much over 40 years?
choices: Money paid in fees can't keep growing for you
quiz.why: Fees compound too: what you pay can't earn growth later.

quiz.q: Two similar funds differ only in fees. Over 30 years, the lower-fee one…
choices: Leaves more of any growth in your account
quiz.why: Lower costs leave more of whatever the fund earns.

lessons.title: Account types: where investments live
objectives: Name the main types of accounts that can hold investments
Explain what ‘tax-advantaged’ means
key_points: A regular brokerage account is flexible, but you may owe tax on gains and dividends
Retirement accounts like 401(k)s and IRAs give tax breaks but limit early withdrawals
The account is the container; the investments inside it are a separate choice
lessons.risk_note: Tax breaks don't protect against losses. Investments in any account can fall in value.

try_it.prompt: List the accounts you already have, and note whether each is a bank, retirement or regular investing account.

quiz.q: What's the difference between an account and an investment?
choices: The account holds investments; what's inside is a separate choice
quiz.why: A retirement account can hold cash, funds or other investments.

quiz.q: A main trade-off of retirement accounts is…
choices: Tax breaks, in exchange for limits on early withdrawals
quiz.why: The tax breaks come with rules about when you can take money out.

quiz.q: In a regular taxable brokerage account…
choices: You may owe tax on gains and dividends
quiz.why: Taxable accounts are flexible, but gains and dividends can be taxed.

lessons.title: Before you open an investing account: what to check
objectives: List the questions to ask before opening an account
Explain what SIPC protection does and doesn't cover
Explain how to check that a firm is registered
key_points: Check the costs: account fees, trading costs and the funds' expense ratios
SIPC protection can help if a brokerage firm fails, but not if investments lose value
You can look up a firm or broker for free on FINRA BrokerCheck
lessons.risk_note: No account type or firm protects you from market losses. Investments can fall in value.

try_it.prompt: Write down three questions you'd ask any firm before opening an account.

quiz.q: What does SIPC protection cover?
choices: Some losses if a brokerage firm fails and customer assets are missing
quiz.why: SIPC doesn't cover market losses.

quiz.q: Where can you check whether a broker is registered?
quiz.why: BrokerCheck is a free public lookup run by FINRA.

quiz.q: Which question is most useful before opening an account?
choices: What does the firm's newest ad say?
How many people follow it online?
What will I pay in account, trading and fund costs?
quiz.why: Costs come out of your money every year.

levels.title: Building a long-term plan
levels.summary: Workplace plans, IRAs and HSAs, choosing a mix, and putting good habits on autopilot.

modules.title: Retirement and health accounts
modules.summary: How 401(k)s, employer matches, IRAs and HSAs work.

lessons.title: How a 401(k) works
objectives: Explain how 401(k) contributions come out of your paycheck
Compare traditional (pre-tax) and Roth contributions
Explain the yearly contribution limit
key_points: You choose a share of each paycheck to go into the plan automatically
Traditional contributions lower your taxes now; Roth contributions can mean tax-free withdrawals later, if the rules are met
There's a yearly limit on how much you can put in, announced by the IRS
lessons.risk_note: Money in a 401(k) is invested and can lose value. Withdrawing early can mean taxes and penalties.

try_it.prompt: Enter the monthly amount you'd put in, and compare starting now with waiting 3 years.

quiz.q: How does money usually get into a 401(k)?
choices: Your bank moves it without asking
quiz.why: Contributions are taken from your pay before it reaches you.

quiz.q: Traditional vs. Roth 401(k): the main difference is…
choices: Only one of them can lose value
When you pay income tax: now or later
quiz.why: Traditional saves tax now; Roth can save tax later.

quiz.q: Who announces the yearly 401(k) contribution limit?
choices: Your employer, at any amount it likes
quiz.why: The IRS publishes the limits, usually each fall for the next year.

lessons.title: What a 401(k) match is, and why people call it “free money”
objectives: Explain how an employer match works
Explain what vesting means
key_points: Some employers add money to your account when you contribute, up to a set amount
For example, a plan might add 50 cents per dollar you put in, up to 6% of your pay (hypothetical)
Vesting rules decide when the employer's money is fully yours
lessons.risk_note: The match goes into an account that's invested and can fall in value. The formula here is a hypothetical example; your plan's documents have the real one.

try_it.prompt: Find your plan's match formula and vesting schedule in your benefits papers and add them to your Money Map.

quiz.q: Hypothetically, a plan adds 50 cents per dollar up to 6% of pay. You earn $40,000 and put in 6%. What's the match for the year?
quiz.why: 6% of $40,000 is $2,400, and half of that is $1,200.

quiz.q: What does vesting mean?
choices: When the employer's contributions become fully yours
When you can first log in
The day your salary is paid
quiz.why: Your own contributions are always yours; vesting applies to the employer's money.

quiz.q: If you put in less than the amount the match is based on, what happens?
choices: You get the full match anyway
quiz.why: The match is tied to what you contribute.

lessons.title: IRAs and Roth IRAs: when you pay the tax
objectives: Explain what an IRA is
Compare traditional and Roth IRAs
Explain the yearly limit and the income rules for Roth IRAs
key_points: An IRA is a retirement account you open yourself, separate from work
Traditional: a possible tax break now. Roth: you pay tax now, and qualified withdrawals can be tax-free later
There's a yearly limit, and who can put money into a Roth IRA depends on income
lessons.risk_note: An IRA is a tax wrapper, not an investment: what's inside can lose value. Tax rules here are general; check IRS.gov or a tax professional for your situation.

try_it.prompt: Enter a monthly amount you could set aside for an IRA, and compare starting now with waiting 5 years.

quiz.q: Who opens an IRA?
choices: Only a bank, on your behalf
quiz.why: IRA stands for individual retirement account.

quiz.q: With a Roth IRA, you…
choices: Never pay any tax on anything
Pay tax now, and qualified withdrawals later can be tax-free
Get a tax break now and pay tax later
quiz.why: That's the Roth trade: tax now, not later.

quiz.q: What can limit who can put money into a Roth IRA?
quiz.why: Roth IRAs have income limits set by the IRS.

lessons.title: HSA basics: a health account with tax breaks
objectives: Explain who can open an HSA
Explain the three tax breaks of an HSA
key_points: An HSA is for people covered by an eligible high-deductible health plan
Money can go in tax-free, grow tax-free, and come out tax-free for qualified medical costs
Unused money stays yours from year to year, and some people invest it
lessons.risk_note: HSA money that's invested can lose value. Tax rules here are federal and general; some states treat HSAs differently, so check IRS.gov for your situation.

try_it.prompt: Check whether your health plan is HSA-eligible, and note what you spent on medical costs last year.

quiz.q: Who can contribute to an HSA?
choices: People covered by an eligible high-deductible health plan
quiz.why: HSAs are tied to specific health plans.

quiz.q: HSA withdrawals are tax-free when used for…
quiz.why: Other uses can mean taxes and penalties.

quiz.q: What happens to unused HSA money at the end of the year?
quiz.why: Unlike many flexible spending accounts, HSA money rolls over.

modules.title: Choosing and keeping a mix
modules.summary: Asset allocation, rebalancing and target-date funds, as ideas.

lessons.title: Asset allocation: your mix of stocks, bonds and cash
objectives: Explain asset allocation
Explain how time horizon and comfort with swings shape a mix
key_points: Asset allocation is how money is split between stocks, bonds and cash
More stocks usually means bigger swings; more bonds and cash usually means smaller ones
When you'll need the money, and how you handle drops, both shape a mix
lessons.risk_note: Every mix can lose value. Mixes in this lesson explain the idea; they aren't suggestions for you.

try_it.prompt: For each goal in your Money Map, note when you'll need the money: under 3 years, 3 to 10 years, or more than 10.

quiz.q: Asset allocation means…
choices: How your money is split between stocks, bonds and cash
quiz.why: It's the overall mix, not any single pick.

quiz.q: A mix with more stocks usually has…
quiz.why: Stocks usually swing more than bonds and cash.

quiz.q: Which matters when thinking about a mix?
choices: When you'll need the money and how you handle drops
quiz.why: Time horizon and comfort with drops shape a mix.

lessons.title: Rebalancing: why your mix drifts
objectives: Explain why a mix drifts over time
Describe two common ways people rebalance
key_points: When some investments grow faster than others, your mix drifts
Rebalancing means moving back toward the mix you chose
Some people rebalance on a schedule, others when the mix drifts past a set amount
lessons.risk_note: Rebalancing doesn't prevent losses, and selling in a taxable account can create taxes.

try_it.prompt: Picture a mix that started half stocks and half bonds. After stocks jump, what would rebalancing do?

quiz.q: Why does a mix drift?
choices: Different investments grow at different speeds
quiz.why: Uneven growth changes the proportions.

quiz.q: After stocks rose a lot, rebalancing would usually mean…
choices: Selling some stocks and adding to bonds or cash
quiz.why: It moves the mix back to where it started.

quiz.q: Which is a common way to rebalance?
choices: On a set schedule, like once a year
quiz.why: A schedule or a drift limit keeps it rule-based.

lessons.title: Target-date funds, as a concept
objectives: Explain how a target-date fund changes its mix over time
Explain why two funds with the same date can differ
key_points: A target-date fund holds a mix that gets more cautious as its target year nears
Funds with the same target year can hold different mixes and charge different fees
The target date isn't a promise: the fund can lose value, even near or after that year
lessons.risk_note: Target-date funds can lose value at any time, including near the target date. This explains the idea; it isn't a recommendation.

try_it.prompt: If your workplace plan offers target-date funds, look up how the mix changes over time (often called the glide path).

quiz.q: A target-date fund's mix usually…
choices: Gets more cautious as the target year nears
quiz.why: The shift over time is called the glide path.

quiz.q: Two funds with the same target year…
choices: Are certain to end at the same value
Can hold different mixes and charge different fees
quiz.why: Always compare the mix and the fees.

quiz.q: What does the target date mean?
choices: The fund is certain to reach a goal by then
The year the fund's mix is designed around, often a retirement year
quiz.why: It's a planning date, not a promise.

modules.title: Putting it on autopilot
modules.summary: Automating good habits and pulling your plan onto one page.

lessons.title: Automating your money: pay future you first
objectives: Explain why automatic transfers help people stick to a plan
Explain investing a set amount on a schedule
key_points: Automatic transfers on payday move money before you can spend it
Investing the same amount on a schedule is called dollar-cost averaging
Small automatic increases, like after a raise, add up over time
lessons.risk_note: Investing on a schedule doesn't prevent losses. Investments can fall in value, including money you put in.

try_it.prompt: Try raising your monthly amount by $25 and see how the hypothetical result changes.

quiz.q: Why do automatic transfers help?
choices: Money moves before you can spend it
quiz.why: Automation takes willpower out of it.

quiz.q: Dollar-cost averaging means…
choices: Investing a set amount on a regular schedule
quiz.why: The same amount goes in at regular times, whatever prices do.

quiz.q: Does investing on a schedule prevent losses?
quiz.why: It can smooth the price you pay, but losses are still possible.

lessons.title: Your money plan on one page
objectives: Put the pieces of a money plan in an order that makes sense to you
Explain why a plan gets reviewed, not set once
key_points: Many plans follow a similar order: cushion, high-interest debt, any match, then other goals
Write down each goal, its timeline, and where its money lives
Check in once or twice a year, or when life changes
lessons.risk_note: This is a general framework, not advice for your situation. Investments can fall in value.

try_it.prompt: Fill in your one-page plan: goals, timelines, accounts and monthly amounts.

quiz.q: Why put a plan on one page?
choices: To see goals, timelines and accounts together
quiz.why: One view makes trade-offs easier to see.

quiz.q: A common order many plans follow starts with…
choices: A cash cushion and high-interest debt
quiz.why: Those steps protect the rest of the plan.

quiz.q: When is it worth revisiting your plan?
choices: Once or twice a year, or when life changes
quiz.why: Plans change as your life does.

levels.title: Advanced investor
levels.summary: Bonds, interest rates and inflation, how investments are taxed, and how markets and minds behave in a crash.

modules.title: Bonds, rates and inflation
modules.summary: How bonds work, why interest rates move their prices, and what inflation does to money.

lessons.title: How bonds work: lending with an end date
objectives: Explain a bond's face value, interest payments and maturity
Explain credit risk: the chance a borrower can't pay
key_points: A bond is a loan: the issuer pays interest and plans to repay the face value at maturity
Government and company bonds differ in how likely the borrower is to pay
Higher interest usually comes with more risk that the borrower won't pay
lessons.risk_note: Bonds can lose value, and a borrower can fail to pay. Most bond funds have no maturity date, so their value keeps moving.

try_it.prompt: Look at the mix in your Money Map and note which part, if any, is in bonds.

quiz.q: A bond's maturity is…
choices: When the issuer plans to repay the face value
quiz.why: Maturity is the bond's end date.

quiz.q: Credit risk is the chance that…
choices: The borrower can't pay as promised
quiz.why: Weaker borrowers carry more credit risk.

quiz.q: Why might one bond pay more interest than another?
choices: Its borrower is seen as riskier
quiz.why: Investors want extra interest for extra risk.

lessons.title: Why bond prices fall when interest rates rise
objectives: Explain the seesaw between interest rates and bond prices
Explain why longer-term bonds swing more
key_points: When rates rise, older bonds paying less become less valuable, so their prices fall
When rates fall, older bonds paying more become more valuable
Longer-term bonds usually swing more when rates change
lessons.risk_note: Bonds and bond funds can lose value, especially when interest rates rise quickly.

try_it.prompt: Picture a hypothetical old bond paying 2% when new ones pay 5%. Would a buyer pay full price for it?

quiz.q: If interest rates rise, prices of existing bonds usually…
quiz.why: Rates and bond prices move like a seesaw.

quiz.q: Why do older bonds lose value when rates rise?
choices: New bonds pay more, so older ones paying less are less attractive
quiz.why: Buyers compare old bonds with new ones.

quiz.q: Which usually swings more when rates change?
quiz.why: The longer the bond, the more a rate change matters.

lessons.title: Inflation: why a dollar buys less over time
objectives: Explain inflation and how it's measured
Explain the difference between nominal and real returns
key_points: Inflation is the general rise in prices, which makes each dollar buy less
In the U.S., the Bureau of Labor Statistics tracks it with the Consumer Price Index
A real return is growth after inflation, which is what changes what you can buy
lessons.risk_note: Investments meant to outpace inflation can still lose value, and nobody knows inflation's future path.

try_it.prompt: Run your numbers, then lower the growth rate by 3 points as a rough, hypothetical stand-in for inflation.

quiz.q: Inflation means…
quiz.why: Each dollar buys a little less.

quiz.q: Hypothetically, an account grows 4% in a year while prices rise 3%. Real growth is about…
quiz.why: Real growth is roughly growth minus inflation: 4% minus 3%.

quiz.q: Cash kept under a mattress during inflation…
quiz.why: The amount stays the same while prices rise.

modules.title: Taxes and fund details
modules.summary: How investments are taxed, what total return means, and how to read a fund fact sheet.

lessons.title: Taxes on investments: gains, dividends and time held
objectives: Explain when selling an investment can create tax
Compare short-term and long-term capital gains
Explain why account type changes the tax picture
key_points: In a regular taxable account, a gain is usually taxed when you sell
Long-term gains are often taxed at lower rates than short-term gains
Retirement accounts and HSAs follow their own tax rules
lessons.risk_note: Tax rules change and depend on your situation. This is general education; check IRS.gov or a tax professional. Investments can lose value.

try_it.prompt: If you have a tax form from an investing account, find the lines for gains and dividends.

quiz.q: In a regular taxable account, a gain is usually taxed when…
quiz.why: A gain on paper usually isn't taxed until you sell.

quiz.q: Long-term capital gains are often taxed…
choices: At higher rates than short-term gains
At lower rates than short-term gains
quiz.why: How long you held something can change the rate.

quiz.q: Dividends in a regular taxable account are usually…
choices: Taxed in the year you receive them
quiz.why: Dividends count as income in the year they're paid.

lessons.title: Dividends and total return
objectives: Explain what a dividend is
Explain total return as price change plus income
key_points: A dividend is a cash payment some companies make to shareholders
When a dividend is paid, the share price usually drops by about that amount
Total return counts both price change and income, so it's the fairer way to compare
lessons.risk_note: Dividends can be cut or stopped at any time, and share prices can fall. Past returns don't predict future ones.

try_it.prompt: Next time you see a fund's past results, check whether they show total return or price change only.

quiz.q: A dividend is…
choices: A cash payment some companies make to shareholders
quiz.why: Companies can choose to pay out part of their profits.

quiz.q: When a company pays a dividend, its share price usually…
quiz.why: Money paid out leaves the company, so the price adjusts.

quiz.q: Total return includes…
choices: Price change plus dividends and interest
quiz.why: It counts everything an investment produced.

lessons.title: Reading a fund fact sheet
objectives: Find a fund's fees, holdings and benchmark on a fact sheet
Explain why past performance doesn't predict future results
key_points: Look for the expense ratio, the top holdings and how many holdings there are
The benchmark is the index the fund is compared with
Past performance is shown, but it doesn't predict future results
lessons.risk_note: A fact sheet describes a fund; it isn't a recommendation. Funds can lose value.

try_it.prompt: Find any fund fact sheet and locate five things: expense ratio, holdings, benchmark, turnover and total return.

quiz.q: Where would you look for what a fund costs each year?
quiz.why: The expense ratio is the yearly cost.

quiz.q: A fund's benchmark is…
quiz.why: The benchmark shows what the fund is measured against.

quiz.q: What does strong past performance tell you about next year?
choices: Nothing certain: past results don't predict future ones
quiz.why: Strong periods can be followed by weak ones.

modules.title: Markets and your mind
modules.summary: What past crashes looked like, why timing is hard, and the mind traps that cost people money.

lessons.title: Market crashes: 2000, 2008, 2020 and 2022
objectives: Describe four major U.S. market drops and what set them off
Explain why recovery times have varied so much
key_points: Big drops have happened many times, each with a different cause
Some recoveries took months; others took years
Nobody knows in advance when a drop will start or end
lessons.risk_note: Past crashes don't predict future ones. A future drop could be bigger or last longer than any of these.

try_it.prompt: Live through a hypothetical crash with a pretend index portfolio, and note what holding and selling would have done.

quiz.q: What do the drops of 2000, 2008, 2020 and 2022 have in common?
choices: Each was a big drop, with a different cause
They all ended within a week
quiz.why: Tech stocks, a financial crisis, a pandemic, then inflation and rising rates.

quiz.q: How long did recoveries take?
choices: It varied, from months to years
quiz.why: Each recovery had its own pace.

quiz.q: Which is true about the next crash?
choices: Nobody knows when it will come or how deep it will be
Experts can predict the exact date
quiz.why: Drops don't follow a timetable.

lessons.title: Why “waiting for the dip” is harder than it sounds
objectives: Explain why timing the market means being right twice
Explain why missing a few strong days can matter
key_points: Timing the market means being right twice: when to get out and when to get back in
Big up days and big down days often come close together, in the same rough stretch
A plan written in calm times can make drops easier to sit through
lessons.risk_note: Holding through a drop doesn't prevent losses, and selling can make sense for someone who needs the money. Investments can fall in value.

try_it.prompt: Run a hypothetical crash twice, once holding and once selling at the low point, and compare the results.

quiz.q: Why is market timing hard?
choices: You have to be right about when to get out and when to get back in
quiz.why: Two correct calls in a row is a lot harder than one.

quiz.q: What has often happened around the worst days in the market?
choices: Some of the best days came close by
quiz.why: People who sold after a bad day sometimes missed the rebound days.

quiz.q: What can make a drop easier to sit through?
choices: A plan written ahead of time, in calm conditions
quiz.why: Decisions made in calm times tend to be clearer.

lessons.title: Mind traps: the biases that cost people money
objectives: Name common biases, like loss aversion, herd behavior and recency bias
Explain one way to notice each of them in yourself
key_points: Losses feel worse than equal gains feel good, which can push people to sell in a panic
Following the crowd and fear of missing out can push people to buy after big run-ups
Recent events feel more likely to repeat than they really are
lessons.risk_note: Knowing about biases doesn't remove risk. Investments can fall in value.

try_it.prompt: Run a crash and write down, at the lowest point, what you felt like doing.

quiz.q: Loss aversion means…
choices: Losses feel worse than equal gains feel good
quiz.why: This feeling can push people to sell at the worst time.

quiz.q: Buying something because everyone else is buying is called…
quiz.why: Crowds can push prices far in either direction.

quiz.q: Recency bias makes people…
choices: Expect recent events to keep repeating
quiz.why: The latest trend feels more permanent than it is.

levels.title: Expert topics explained
levels.summary: How leverage, options, crypto and real estate work and how they can hurt, plus retirement math, estate basics and spotting scams. Explained, never recommended.

modules.title: High-risk products, explained
modules.summary: How leverage, options and crypto work, and why beginners get hurt.

lessons.title: Leverage: how borrowing magnifies gains and losses
objectives: Explain how borrowing to invest magnifies both gains and losses
Explain a margin call
Explain why leveraged funds can drift from what people expect
key_points: Leverage means investing with borrowed money, so gains and losses both get bigger
If a margin account falls too far, the firm can demand more cash or sell your holdings
Leveraged funds reset daily, so over longer periods results can differ a lot from what people expect
lessons.risk_note: Leverage can lose more than you put in. This lesson explains how it works; it isn't a strategy to use.

try_it.prompt: Work through a hypothetical: $1,000 of your own money plus $1,000 borrowed, and the investment falls by half. What's left of your money?

quiz.q: Leverage makes…
quiz.why: Borrowing magnifies results in both directions.

quiz.q: Hypothetically, you invest $1,000 of your own plus $1,000 borrowed. The investment falls by half. After repaying the loan, how much of your own money is left?
quiz.why: $2,000 falls to $1,000, and all of it goes to repay the loan.

quiz.q: A margin call is…
choices: A phone call offering a bonus
A demand for more cash, or a forced sale, when a margin account falls too far
quiz.why: The firm can sell your holdings without waiting for you.

lessons.title: Options: how calls and puts work
objectives: Explain what call and put options are
Explain premium, strike price and expiration
Explain why an option can expire worthless
key_points: An option is a contract giving the right, not the duty, to buy (call) or sell (put) at a set price by a set date
The buyer pays a premium; if the option expires worthless, that premium is gone
Options lose value as time passes, even if the stock price doesn't move
lessons.risk_note: Options are complex and risky. Buyers can lose everything they paid, and some option sellers can lose far more. Explained here, never recommended.

try_it.prompt: Read a hypothetical: a call with a $50 strike price that cost $2. Above what price does the buyer come out ahead at expiration?

quiz.q: A call option gives the buyer the right to…
choices: Sell at a set price by a set date
Buy at a set price by a set date
quiz.why: A put is the right to sell.

quiz.q: If an option expires worthless, the buyer…
choices: Receives a refund from the exchange
quiz.why: The premium is the price of the contract, and it's gone.

quiz.q: Hypothetically, a call has a $50 strike and cost $2. At expiration, the stock must be above what price for the buyer to come out ahead?
quiz.why: The buyer needs the strike plus the premium: $50 plus $2, ignoring fees.

lessons.title: How options can hurt beginners
objectives: Explain how time decay and leverage work against option buyers
Explain why selling options can mean very large losses
Explain why brokers have to approve options trading
key_points: A small move in the stock can mean a big swing in an option's value
Time works against option buyers: value drains away as expiration nears
Some option-selling positions can lose far more than the money received
lessons.risk_note: Options can lose all their value quickly, and some positions can lose more than you put in. Brokers must give the official options risk disclosure before approving an account.

try_it.prompt: Read the opening pages of the official options disclosure, “Characteristics and Risks of Standardized Options,” and list two risks it names.

quiz.q: As expiration nears, an option's time value…
quiz.why: This is called time decay.

quiz.q: Why can an option's value swing so much?
choices: A small move in the stock can mean a big move in the option
quiz.why: Options work like leverage.

quiz.q: Before approving options trading, a broker must…
choices: Give you the official options risk disclosure
quiz.why: Approval also depends on your experience and finances.

lessons.title: Crypto: how it works and what can go wrong
objectives: Explain what a cryptocurrency and a blockchain are
Name the main risks: price swings, hacks, scams and platform failures
Explain why crypto on an app isn't like money in an insured bank
key_points: Crypto is digital money recorded on a shared ledger called a blockchain
Prices can swing wildly, and coins can lose most or all of their value
Crypto isn't covered by bank deposit insurance, and transfers usually can't be reversed
lessons.risk_note: Crypto is highly speculative and can lose all its value. Explained here, never recommended.

try_it.prompt: If you hold any crypto, note in your Money Map where it's held and who controls the keys.

quiz.q: A blockchain is…
choices: A shared digital record of transactions
quiz.why: It's a ledger copied across many computers.

quiz.q: If a crypto platform fails, bank deposit insurance…
quiz.why: Deposit insurance covers bank deposits, not crypto.

quiz.q: If you send crypto to a scammer, can you usually reverse it?
choices: Usually not: crypto transfers are hard to reverse
Yes, your bank will refund it
quiz.why: That's why scammers often ask for crypto.

modules.title: The long game
modules.summary: Real estate, making savings last in retirement, and naming who gets your money.

lessons.title: Real estate and REITs: the basics
objectives: Explain the difference between a home you live in and property owned as an investment
Explain what a REIT is
Name the risks of real estate: borrowing, costs and being hard to sell
key_points: A home is a place to live with big ongoing costs, not only an investment
A REIT is a company that owns property; many trade on exchanges like stocks
Property often involves a mortgage, which is leverage, and can be slow and costly to sell
lessons.risk_note: Property values and REITs can fall, and borrowing magnifies losses. Non-traded REITs can be hard to sell. Explained here, not recommended.

try_it.prompt: List the true monthly costs of where you live: payment or rent, insurance, taxes, repairs and fees.

quiz.q: A REIT is…
choices: A company that owns property, often traded like a stock
quiz.why: REIT stands for real estate investment trust.

quiz.q: Which is a real cost of owning a home beyond the mortgage?
quiz.why: Ongoing costs are part of the true price.

quiz.q: Why is a property hard to sell quickly?
choices: It's illegal to sell within ten years
Selling takes time and comes with big costs
quiz.why: Property is far less liquid than a fund.

lessons.title: Retirement withdrawal math: making savings last
objectives: Explain what a withdrawal rate is
Explain sequence-of-returns risk
Explain why rules of thumb aren't promises
key_points: A withdrawal rate is the share of savings taken out each year
Big losses early in retirement hurt more than the same losses later
Popular rules of thumb come from studies of past markets, and they aren't promises
lessons.risk_note: Savings can run out if returns are poor or withdrawals are high. This is general education, not advice for your situation.

try_it.prompt: Picture two retirees with the same savings: one hits a crash in year one, the other in year fifteen. Whose savings are under more strain, and why?

quiz.q: Hypothetically, someone takes $20,000 a year from $500,000 in savings. What's the withdrawal rate?
Sequence-of-returns risk means…
choices: Returns arrive in a fixed order
The order of good and bad years matters once withdrawals start
quiz.why: Selling during an early drop leaves less to recover with.

quiz.q: Rules of thumb for retirement withdrawals…
choices: Work the same in every market
Come from past data and aren't promises
quiz.why: The future can differ from the past.

lessons.title: Beneficiaries and estate basics
objectives: Explain what a beneficiary designation is
Explain why beneficiary forms can matter more than a will for some accounts
Name the basic documents: will, power of attorney and health care directive
key_points: A beneficiary is the person you name to receive an account or policy if you die
For many retirement accounts and insurance policies, the beneficiary form decides who gets the money, even over a will
A will, a financial power of attorney and a health care directive are where many adults start; rules vary by state

try_it.prompt: List each account and policy you have, and note whether a beneficiary is named and who it is.

quiz.q: A beneficiary is…
choices: The person you name to receive an account if you die
quiz.why: You name beneficiaries on the account's own form.

quiz.q: For many retirement accounts, what usually decides who receives the money?
quiz.why: The form usually controls, even if a will says something else.

quiz.q: Why review beneficiaries after big life changes?
choices: An old form can send money to someone you didn't intend
quiz.why: Marriage, divorce or a new child are common reasons to update.

modules.title: Protecting yourself
modules.summary: Spotting scams and hype, and checking anyone who offers money advice.

lessons.title: Spotting investment scams
objectives: Name the warning signs of an investment scam
Explain how to check a person or firm before handing over money
Explain where to report a suspected scam
key_points: Anyone promising high returns with little risk is waving a classic red flag
Pressure to decide fast, secrecy, and requests to pay in crypto or gift cards are warning signs
Check registration on FINRA BrokerCheck or the SEC's adviser search, and report scams to the SEC or the FTC
lessons.risk_note: Every investment can lose value. Anyone who says otherwise is showing a red flag.

try_it.prompt: Look up one person or firm you've seen online on FINRA BrokerCheck or the SEC's adviser search.

quiz.q: Which is a classic red flag?
choices: A registered firm that explains its fees
Pressure to decide today and keep it secret
A written explanation of the risks
quiz.why: Real opportunities don't need secrecy or a deadline.

quiz.q: Someone asks you to pay for an investment with gift cards. This is…
choices: A common sign of a scam
quiz.why: Legitimate firms don't take gift cards.

quiz.q: Where can you report a suspected investment scam?
choices: Only to the person who pitched it
quiz.why: Reports help regulators stop scams.

lessons.title: Hype, finfluencers and red flags online
objectives: Recognize hype language and pressure tactics online
Explain why paid promotions and cherry-picked results mislead
Explain how to slow down before acting on a tip
key_points: Phrases like “to the moon,” “can't lose” and “act now” are red flags
Creators may be paid to promote something, and they may show only their wins
A tip that makes you feel rushed is a reason to pause, not to act
lessons.risk_note: No one can promise returns. Any investment can lose value.

try_it.prompt: Pick one money video from your feed and check: is it paid, does it show losses, and does it rush you?

quiz.q: Which is a warning sign in a money video?
choices: It shows losses as well as gains
It promises big gains in a short time
quiz.why: Promised gains are a classic hype signal.

quiz.q: Why can a creator's results be misleading?
choices: They may show only wins, or be paid to promote
quiz.why: What you see is often a highlight reel.

quiz.q: A tip makes you feel rushed. A sensible first step is…
choices: Pausing to check the source and the risks
quiz.why: Urgency is a pressure tactic, not information.

lessons.title: Getting help: checking who gives money advice
objectives: Explain the difference between an adviser's duty and a salesperson's
Explain how advisers get paid and why it matters
Explain how to look up an adviser's record
key_points: Investment advisers owe clients a fiduciary duty; brokers follow a different standard, and job titles alone won't tell you which
Advisers may be paid flat fees, a share of your assets, or commissions on products they sell
You can look up registration and any disciplinary history on FINRA BrokerCheck or the SEC's adviser search
lessons.risk_note: Good advice can't remove investment risk. Investments can fall in value.

try_it.prompt: Write down three questions for any adviser: how are you paid, are you a fiduciary, and where can I see your record?

quiz.q: Why does it matter how an adviser is paid?
choices: Pay can create conflicts, like commissions on products sold
quiz.why: Knowing how someone is paid shows their incentives.

quiz.q: Can you tell an adviser's legal duty from their job title alone?
choices: Yes, all titles are strictly regulated
Yes, if the title includes the word ‘wealth’
Not always: ask, and check their registration
quiz.why: Many titles aren't regulated.

quiz.q: Where can you look up a broker's or adviser's record?
choices: FINRA BrokerCheck or the SEC's adviser search
quiz.why: Both are free public lookups.
